newsitem.title: UK: Sweeping British gun ban runs into trouble.
newsitem.headline: Sweeping British gun ban runs into trouble.

text.p: The British government unveiled plans on Wednesday to outlaw most handguns in response to the massacre in the Scottish town of Dunblane when a crazed loner shot dead 16 young children and their teacher.

But Prime Minister John Major immediately came under fierce pressure from opposition politicians, anti-gun campaigners and some members of his own Conservative Party to go even further and push through a blanket ban on handguns.
Ministers said they planned to legislate by Christmas to ban at least 80 percent of Britain's 200,000 legally held handguns.
The only handguns Britons would be allowed are single-shot .22-inch calibre weapons, widely used in shooting competitions.
These would have to be held under lock and key at gun clubs, which would have to meet stringent new security standards.

"The package of measures I have announced today will give this country some of the toughest gun control laws in the world," Home Secretary Michael Howard, the interior minister, told parliament. "The country expects nothing less."

Howard said it would become harder for individuals to obtain licences. He also proposed a ban on mail-order purchases of firearms and the sale of expanding ammunition of the type Thomas Hamilton, a loner with a worrying fondness for young boys, used in March in a slaughter of the innocents that shocked the world.
Hamilton then turned one of his four semi-automatic pistols -- all legally obtained -- on himself.
"I conclude that this was an act of calculated wickedness," Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth, whose parliamentary constituency includes Dunblane, told a sombre chamber.
Forsyth proposed a raft of complementary measures including improved security at schools and closer vetting and supervising of adults working with children and young people.
He also announced the resignation of the Scottish police inspector who had granted Hamilton a gun licence.

The government's proposals go beyond the recommendations of a senior judge, Lord Douglas Cullen, who conducted an inquiry into the massacre. Cullen's main proposal was to require handguns to be kept at gun clubs and not at home.
Major, with a majority of just two in the 651-seat lower House of Commons, was advised that he risked defeat in parliament unless he went much further.
Immediate reaction from his own members of parliament suggested, however, that the government could struggle to win approval for anything less than a blanket ban.
Demanding a free vote, former Conservative minister David Mellor said: "It is time to conclude that, literally and metaphorically, the game is up for handguns now. That is the public will."
Dunblane parents who have collected 750,000 signatures on a petition seeking a blanket ban on handguns said they would keep up pressure on ministers.
"I want them to go one further step forward so that we have a total ban on handguns," Mick North, whose daughter Sophie was one of Hamilton's victims, told BBC television.
The main opposition Labour Party said it too would press for a complete ban -- a position it arrived at following an emotional appeal to its annual conference by a Dunblane mother.
"There is no place in any decent, civilised society for handguns of any kind," Labour's Scottish affairs spokesman, George Robertson, said.

"Let us therefore resolve that the lasting legacy of the evil which visited Dunblane on March 13 will be the complete outlawing of handguns," said Robertson, whose children attended the school where the massacre occurred.
Gun lobbyists argue that most of the 57,000 holders of handgun licences practise target shooting and should not have to pay for the actions of one deranged gunman.
"It's not the guns that are the problem, it's the people who use those guns illegally," Conservative member of parliament John Carlisle, who attacked the proposed clampdown, said.
It was the second time within months that a developed country has cracked down on firearms following a mass slaughter.

In July, Australian Prime Minister John Howard won national agreement for laws banning self-loading guns and tightening firearm ownership rules after 35 people were shot dead at the Port Arthur tourist site on the island of Tasmania on April 28.
